blocks.text: Filtration separates one component of a two-component heterogeneous mixture from a solution. First a suitable solvent is chosen in which one component dissolves completely while the other remains practically insoluble. For a mixture of common salt and sand, the mixture is dissolved in distilled water: the salt distributes itself throughout the water to give a homogeneous mixture, a solution of common salt in water, while the sand remains undissolved and settles. The salt is the solute and the water the solvent, the solvent being the component present in excess. Filtration then separates the sand.

blocks.title: Solute, solvent, solution, filtrate and residue
blocks.text: In a solution the dissolved substance is the solute and the liquid in excess the solvent. After filtration the liquid collected in the flask below the funnel is the filtrate, and the solid left on the filter is the residue.

blocks.long_description: To separate sand from salt the mixture is stirred into water, which dissolves the salt and leaves the sand, and the suspension is poured through a paper cone in a funnel: the sand stays as residue and the clear salt solution passes as filtrate. A fluted paper or a crucible with suction speeds the filtering, and crucibles also serve for precipitates that must be ignited or for solutions that attack paper. Crystallization recovers a pure solid from a solution by dissolving it in a hot solvent that holds little when cold, filtering while hot, cooling slowly so that medium-sized crystals grow, filtering the crystals from the mother liquor under suction and drying them, with charcoal to remove coloured impurities and a desiccator for safe drying.

blocks.text: Filtration through a glass funnel and filter paper is usually slow: as the mixture is poured on, the solvent passes through, leaving the suspended particles on the paper. Filter papers come in various porosities (pore sizes), chosen according to the particle size of the precipitate; the paper should be large enough to be one-quarter to one-half full of precipitate at the end, so that the filtrate runs down the side of the beaker without splashing (Figure 15.1). The paper is folded in half, then in half again, and opened into a cone, inserted into a 60-degree funnel, moistened with water and pressed down (Figure 15.2a). The rate of filtration through a conical funnel is much increased by a fluted filter paper, folded fan-wise with alternate elevations and depressions (Figure 15.2b).

A precipitate can also be filtered by suction through a crucible. A Gooch crucible is porcelain with a perforated bottom covered with paper pulp or a filter paper cut to size (Figure 15.3); placed in a suction apparatus it filters quickly, and it suits precipitates that must be ignited at high temperature; with its perforations covered by an asbestos mat it can filter solutions that react with paper, such as concentrated HCl and KMnO4. A sintered glass crucible has a porous glass disc sealed into the bottom and needs no preparation (Figure 15.4).

blocks.prompt: Name the filter media used, differentiate gravity from vacuum filtration, and the Gooch from the sintered glass crucible (Quick Check 15.1a, c, d; exercise Q.2c).
blocks.explanation: Media: plain and fluted filter paper, the Gooch crucible with paper pulp or asbestos, and the sintered glass crucible. Gravity filtration lets the liquid drain through a paper cone under its own weight and is slow; vacuum filtration pulls it through a crucible by suction and is fast. The Gooch crucible is porcelain with holes that must be covered with pulp or asbestos before use, and it can be ignited; the sintered glass crucible has a built-in porous glass disc, needs no preparation, but cannot be strongly heated.

items: Filtration: dissolve the soluble component (solute) in a solvent, pour through a filter; the insoluble residue stays, the filtrate passes (salt from sand).
Media: paper cone in a 60-degree funnel (slow), fluted paper (fast), Gooch crucible (suction, ignition, asbestos for HCl and KMnO4), sintered glass crucible (no preparation).
